utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the staff of the registry. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please. We haven't been sitting for some time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-98-33-T, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the appearances, please. The Prosecution, Mr. Harmon, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; and good morning, counsel. My name is Mark Harmon and assisting me in the Prosecution is Mr. Peter McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic, please, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence is represented by me, Nenad Petrusic, and my colleague, Mr. Visnjic, Tomislav Visnjic, as has been the case hitherto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We have two decisions, two rulings to make, and we are going to render those rulings orally. And there will be no written ruling. On 26 February 2001, the Defence submitted two motions. The first seeks “to exclude alleged statements of the accused” and the second regards disclosure of exculpatory evidence. The Prosecution opposed the motions when it responded to them on 14 March 2001. The Defence presented a reply in relation to the first motion. I - Motion to exclude alleged statements of the accused The issue concerns recordings of tapped conversations held at the time of the facts on which the Prosecutor contends the voice of General Krstic can be heard (saying in particular “kill them all”) and which the Prosecution would like to have admitted as evidence. The Defence objects to such admission on the ground that: (1) the tapped conversations constitute statements of the accused within the meaning of Rule 66 of the Rules; and (2) the evidence concerns the merits of the case and as such cannot be admitted during the Prosecutor’s rebuttal. (1) The Chamber observes that, by having the Prosecution disclose to the Defence the statements of the accused and of the witnesses, the purpose of Rule 66 of the Rules is to allow for a better preparation of the defence and, generally, for respect for the rights of the Defence. However, the Chamber points out that Rule 66 consists of two major parts. Although Rule 66(A) requires disclosure of the statements of the accused, Rule 66(B) makes it clear that the Prosecutor is in no manner bound to disclose all the books, documents and other evidence in her custody. She is bound to do so only if the Defence initiates the “reciprocal disclosure” procedure laid down in Rule 67 of the Rules. The Prosecution would therefore have been obliged to disclose to the Defence the tapped conversations at issue only if they constituted statements of the accused in the literal sense. Such is not the case. The Chamber is of the view that “statements of the accused” within the meaning of Rule 66 of the Rules are to be understood as the statements made by the accused, spontaneously or not, only when he is aware that what he is saying is being recorded somehow during any type of police or judicial procedure. Such is evidently not the case here. The “tapped conversations” at issue must be dealt with as “documents” within the meaning of Rule 66. The motion is therefore dismissed in this regard. (2) As regards the tardiness of the Prosecutor’s use of the tapped radio conversations, the Chamber regrets that the Prosecution did not present the documents at a more timely moment for the conduct of the whole trial. The documents are incontestably relevant and, assuming that they are admitted, they are among those which clearly concern the merits of the case at least as much as the credibility of the accused. That said and whatever their ultimate probative value, the Chamber observes without however sharing all of the Prosecutor’s reasons that the Defence had a reasonable time to present any objections to the documents. Indeed, the Defence was informed at the beginning of General Krstic’s

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: request that the documents be admitted during her rebuttal. As such, the Defence had sufficient time to prepare itself, in such a way that the principle of balance between the parties cannot be considered to have been breached. Since the documents are therefore relevant, the Chamber will decide on whether to admit them after examining all of the explanations provided by the Prosecution and the Defence during the rebuttal and rejoinder. The Defence’s motion on the tapped radio conversations of General Krstic is thus dismissed. So those are the rulings of the Chamber with respect to the Defence motion to exclude the assumed statements by the accused. We have also stated that it will be necessary to rule on the motion on the disclosure of exculpatory evidence, but before doing so, the Chamber would like to have some clarification on the part of the Defence to see whether we need or not to make a ruling on that question. The information has to do with a note at the bottom of the page of the response of the Defence regarding the motion to the exclusion of statements by the accused, and the footnote, I have the text in English so I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "The Defence also filed a motion for disclosure of exculpatory evidence. It is satisfied from the Prosecutor's disclosures subsequent to filing the motion and from the Prosecutor's representations in their response that the Defence has received the essence of what it sought, evidence that no Muslims were killed as a result of General Krstic's alleged statements on 2 August." [Interpretation] Therefore, I'm going to ask the Defence whether that means that the motion has been withdrawn, is no longer valid, or any other relevant information. Mr. Visnjic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning my learned friends opposite. Mr. President, from the moment the Defence submitted this request or this motion to the present, the Prosecution has in the meantime disclosed to the Defence a certain quantity of documents which would meet almost all the requests of the Defence as listed in our motion. The only thing that remains substantially disputed between the Defence and the Prosecution are the statements of two witnesses, and they are witnesses DB and Obrenovic, with whom the Prosecution has conducted interviews. And in connection with our motion for disclosure, we were informed by the Prosecution that both witnesses during their interview were not questioned at all in connection with the critical intercepts of the 2nd of August. If the Prosecution confirms that to us, in that case we consider that the majority of our requests have been fulfilled and we would therefore withdraw this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, have you any comments to make in response to this statement regarding the withdrawal of the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we understood footnote 1 to be a motion to withdraw the application that had been filed with the Trial Chamber, but in response to the question raised by my colleague Mr. Visnjic, we addressed that issue in paragraph 19 of our motion. I have been informed that in the course of the interviews of two individuals who have been referred to by my colleague, that neither was asked about the conversation in question, and based on that information I then included that in paragraph 19 and confirm it orally today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. So we don't need to make any ruling about this since the Defence has confirmed that it has withdrawn its request. It is now time for us to resume our case. As you have seen, after the Prosecution's rebuttal and the rejoinder of the Defence, we will then decide on the admission of this document which was the object of discussion between the parties. I see that Mr. Visnjic has a question to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wish to notify the Chamber that the Defence intends to appeal this ruling by the Chamber, and therefore the Defence suggests that the proceedings be suspended until a final ruling on appeal. However, in the meantime, we can continue with some other evidence that has been part of the Prosecution's rebuttal case. So I'm referring to the decision rejecting the motion for the elimination of the alleged statements of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any response to make? Not regarding the appeal, but regarding the suggestion for suspension.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we oppose the motion to suspend these proceedings. We have, I think, 15 or 13 witnesses who are coming, who have been scheduled. We are prepared to present their testimony. We have a finite amount of time - one week - in which to present our case and we're prepared to move forward. It would be a huge disruption in the orderly proceedings at this point to suspend the proceedings that have been scheduled to allow the Defence an opportunity to file an appeal. It's their right to file an appeal, they can do so when they want, but to suspend these proceedings would not be a very prudent decision at this point in time and we oppose the application to suspend these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I would just like to -- Mr. Visnjic, I would just like to make sure that you understand -- your understanding is the same as mine of the President's ruling, and that is that thus far his only ruling has been that these intercepts do not fall within Rule 66 definition of a statement. It is yet -- the question of authentication of those, which would be prior to any admission, has not been reached, or indeed the evidence hasn't been put in by the Prosecution; and secondly, we have not yet ruled on whether, despite -- assuming they are properly authenticated, they are indeed appropriately put in in rebuttal as opposed to the case in chief. So those rulings, which will be forthcoming, have not yet been made. I just want to make sure that we all understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must admit that that was not my understanding of the ruling. I have just consulted with my colleague, Mr. Petrusic. So my understanding was that our motion was rejected as a whole. So I now understand it's only the interpretation according to Rule 66 (A). So our motion to suspend would not be appropriate. We are just announcing our intention to file an appeal, and we may perhaps later on make another suggestion, depending on how we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic, too. So we are going to continue our work and our proceedings. And of course you are fully entitled to appeal. I would now like to give the floor to the Prosecutor to present, in line with Rule 85, its rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Our first witness today is Dr. Peter French. He has been asked to review the tape for a voice comparison matching analysis and a voice tamper analysis. We call him as our first witness slightly out of order because he has court engagements in the UK on Wednesday, and so as opposed to the intercept operators that took down this material and listened to these tapes, we would ask him to be the first witness. And because it's slightly out of order, I think I should give you a little bit of background because there is a new exhibit in this case. And as you may recall from the motions that went back and forth in, I think, especially the footnote material, the Prosecution at about shortly before General Krstic's testimony, another team had a consent search of the Bosnian Muslim army archives and where they recovered from the archives in Sarajevo numerous reel-to-reel tapes, much like the tapes that we've already played in evidence. After General Krstic was through testifying, our analysis and review found another version of the so-called August 2nd "kill them all" tape, and so we sent that tape as well as the original tape that you heard to Dr. French for his overall analysis and comparison. So he will be, in speaking to you today, be referring to both tapes, as well as will the other witnesses that you'll be hearing from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does the Defence have the second tape? Do they know about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As soon as we found out about it, we gave them a copy, a transcript, and fully informed them of that tape. And we have actually been working with the Defence and their expert and our expert to make sure they had a full chance to review the material. In fact, their expert did go to the UK and spend two days with our expert reviewing the material, and we have not received a report from their expert yet, but if there is one, we hope to get it. So as far as I know, they are fully apprised of all the material, the notebooks, the printouts, the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, allow me to ask the Defence whether they have any objections outside this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We can then call the witness, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. French, please. And perhaps we could have his CV ready for him. It's Exhibit 840/A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Peter French. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming, Dr. French. You will first be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor. It is Mr. Peter McCloskey, who is standing to your right. Mr. McCloskey, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. French, could you first tell the Court what your professional position is, and then if you could tell the Court your educational background and your training background that led you to that profession.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm an independent forensic consultant specialising in the analysis of tape recordings, speech, and language samples. I have a higher degree in linguistics with phonetics - phonetics being the science of speech sounds - and a doctoral degree - that's a PhD - in the analysis of tape-recorded conversation. I am a member and a fellow of a number of professional associations. I'm currently chairman of the International Association For Forensic Phonetics, and that is the professional association which takes responsibility for work in the area in which I appear today. And I'm -- I was awarded a fellowship of the Institute of Acoustics, acoustics being the physics of sound. I wonder, Mr. McCloskey, rather than actually going through my curriculum vitae a line at a time, I think for purposes of Mr. President and Their Honours, there's probably nothing worse than just listening to someone rattling off their own achievements. Perhaps if they have this in writing, they could take it away and we would save court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's Exhibit 840/A that you should have in front of you, and the Court will also have access to it.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea. Can you briefly, though, tell us, have you testified in court before on your profession?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I say in the written CV that it's about 200 times. I think it's probably around 300 now. I've been consulted in 3.000 or more cases which have involved many more thousands of examinations of individual tapes. In criminal cases, I act for both the Prosecution and Defence I like to say in roughly equal proportions, but I probably do just slightly more Prosecution work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned phonetics and linguistics. Can you give us a brief, a little more detailed brief description of what it is you really do in practical terms for the Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. The work that I do in relation to tape recordings falls into a number of different types. Firstly, if tape recordings are produced which are of bad quality, which are contaminated by noise, I'm asked to filter them, to enhance them, to remove the noise in order to make the conversation more audible or intelligible. I also examine tape recordings for any evidence of their having been tampered with or edited before they're put into court as evidence. I compare voices in recordings. This is called forensic speaker identification work where there will be the voice of a known suspect, usually on one tape, and the voice which is questioned in a criminal recording, so I would compare the voices in order to attempt to identify or eliminate the suspect. In addition to that, I'm sometimes asked to determine what's said on a tape. These are cases where perhaps the person has a very non-standard dialect or they speak English with a very heavy foreign accent or the tape is in some way problematic. What I would do is to undertake a study of those speech patterns and, based on that, examine what's said in the tape and give a view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it your voice expertise is mainly in English, your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you are analysing the voice or language of someone in a foreign tongue, do you generally bring on a consultant that's an expert in that foreign tongue?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. I would want someone who was -- who have thorough knowledge of that language, either as a native speaker or had research knowledge of that language. I would also want that person to be a linguist or a phonetician. The reason that I need someone in that capacity is that, in attempting to identify speakers, one is looking for idiosyncratic or personally distinguishing features of speech, in other words, departures from the norm. In order to identify a departure from the norm, one must know what the norm is for that language or the variety of that language in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this particular case, I believe you consulted with a witness who we will have as a protected witness, so we would refer to him as Witness EE. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did we ask you to do in this particular case, and then what did you review and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I was asked to undertake two main tasks. The first one was to examine a tape recording which occurred on two different open-spool tapes. And I don't know whether we should identify these for the Court now, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. These are the tapes in front of me; one known as, I think, tape 48, and one known as tape 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, tape 48 is Exhibit 789, and that is the new tape you'll be hearing; and tape 49 was Exhibit -- excuse me. Tape 48 was the old tape, the first one you heard, and tape 49 is Exhibit 835, and that is the new tape.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Right. My attention was drawn to a recording of conversation which occurred on both of these tapes, and I was given a transcript of this in which three speakers had been identified, one as General Krstic, one as Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, and one as Lieutenant Colonel Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Dr. French, for interrupting, but I think there's something we must clear up now. I think that you mentioned a tape 48 and 32, I think you mentioned, and Mr. McCloskey spoke of tape 49 and 48. So could we clear that up, please, and the correspondence between those numbers and exhibit numbers. So Mr. McCloskey, please, could you clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President, and I'm sorry. The witness is well familiar with the different numbers that have been assigned to these tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So perhaps you could -- tape 32 is also tape 49, which is Exhibit 835.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is the new tape.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: As I said, there was a transcript of the conversation in question and, on the transcript, speech had been variously attributed to General Krstic, Major Obrenovic, and Major Jevdjevic. I was asked to consult other tapes that were provided to me - these were tape recordings of UN interview proceedings in which the three officers had been interviewed - and to compare the voice and speech patterns found on the questioned recordings with the known voice and speech patterns of the three officers from their interview recordings, the purpose being to try to identify or eliminate them from participation in the questioned conversation, which was an intercepted military radio transmission. I consulted Witness EE over this, Witness EE being an expert in Slavian (sic) languages and in B/C/S in particular. We worked together on this and carried out a number of tests. I should say that in forensic speaker identification and elimination cases, the tests one carries out are normally looked on as falling into two groups. On the one hand, there are tests which are known collectively as auditory phonetic tests, which is perhaps a rather highfalutin way of saying listening tests. They are listening tests which are based on university ear training in phonetics. What one listens for is, firstly, how the individual consonant and vowel sounds are pronounced. So just to give an example, in the ordinary Roman alphabet, which we all use to write with, or most of us use to write with, we have only 26 letters. But in carrying out an auditory phonetic analysis, one has available an extended alphabet which has been developed by the International Phonetic Association for capturing the fine-grained nuances of pronunciation. This would allow one to find discriminations which the Roman alphabet would not. For instance, irrespective of how one pronounces a "T" sound, or "ta", using the Roman alphabet one would have available only one letter "T" for recording how it had been pronounced, whereas using the IPA system, the International Phonetic Association system of symbols, one could discriminate between different subvarieties of "ta" sound; some perhaps made with the tip of the tongue further forward against the upper teeth, some with the tip of the tongue curled backwards, some with the tip of the tongue on the tooth ridge, and so on. And I pick out "T" just as an example. The same would apply to any of the other consonant or vowel sounds. So one part of the auditory phonetic testing involves going through the questioned recordings and the known samples - in this case, the interview recordings - and making a note of how the consonants and vowels are pronounced to see if they match across. Now, that part of the work I think is perhaps better reported on by Witness EE, because there are obvious accent and dialect considerations there and he takes primary responsibility for that element of the report. Also under the auditory phonetic testing one would be listening to the rhythms of the speech, the intonation - that's the rise and fall of pitch across sentences - and to the voice quality. Voice quality refers to the resonances of the speech, whether it's a creaky voice, a husky voice, a breathy voice, a nasal voice, or perhaps, like my voice, an adenoidal voice. People ask me if I've got a cold when I haven't. At the end of the auditory phonetic testing, one would then bring into play another set of tests known as acoustic tests. Nowadays they involve re-recording the samples, the interview samples and the questioned samples, within a computer system and running various programmes to take physical measurements of elements of the speech. So for instance, in this case, we measured the average fundamental frequency. The fundamental frequency refers to the rate at which the vocal cords are vibrating when a person speaks. Behind the Adam's apple, here in the larynx, there are two folds of skin -- two folds of muscle, sorry, known as the vocal folds or the vocal cords, and when we speak, when we produce vowel sounds and certain consonants, these vibrate backwards and forwards very, very rapidly. The more rapid the rate of vibration, the higher the pitch of the voice as we hear it. And this was calculated for both the known samples and the questioned speech attributed to the three officers. It was also possible to undertake a very limited amount of what's known as spectrographic analysis. This involves looking at the distribution of sound energy across voice frequencies across time. But the only person, for reasons I'll come on to at the moment, that it was possible to do any spectrographic work with at all, and that was very limited, was the speech attributed to Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic. I should say in this case the comparisons that we undertook were made rather difficult by two main factors. One was that the radio transmitted speech - this is the questioned recordings on the military intercepts - was a very restricted frequency range. And I don't know whether I may, Mr. President, Your Honours, make references to my notes and report on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I think it is up to you, perhaps, to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. If that would assist your testimony, please do.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I may note for the record, he's written two reports, one involving the examinations of speech, which is OTP Exhibit 839/A, and then the matter which he'll get to a little later, the report on the audio recordings, which is Exhibit 838/A.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned earlier, the recording occurred in two forms, one on each of two tapes. The one on the first tape, as it's been referred to, that's tape 48, there was little speech energy at frequencies above 2.3 kilohertz. That's 2.3 vibrations per second. I used that tape to look at the questioned voice of Major Obrenovic. The other tape, tape 32, there was a slightly better signal on that tape than there was on tape 48 of the speech attributed to General Krstic and Major Jevdjevic. And on that tape there was little speech energy at frequencies higher than 1.7 kilohertz. Now, these are very thin, narrow, restricted frequency bands, and that will become clear if one considers that a telephone conversation, which is also frequency limited, extends normally up to about 3.4 kilohertz. So these were very narrowly restricted in frequency band, which detracts from the quality and it detracts from the amount of analysis that can go into them. So the spectrographic tests could only be done on the voice of questioned Obrenovic on tape 48, and then only a small amount of work looking at energy at the low speech frequencies. The second factor which restricted the amount of testing on the strength of the conclusions was the fact that in the military interceptions, the people appeared to be shouting. This was less so perhaps with General Krstic than with the other two speakers, but the quality was very much like "dobro! dobro! dobro!" It was strained and it was shouted as though people were transmitting over long distances. And again, that limited the amount of testing because one was comparing those voices with voices in interviews where people were speaking in a rather slow, deliberate and measured way. At the end of the testing, the results were inconclusive. None of the tests that we carried out would allow us to identify any of the three officers, even as a matter of probability. The most that can be said is that we couldn't eliminate them. There were some similarities in voice quality, but these were difficult to assess because of the shouting versus non-shouting. The shouting also affected the pitch of the voice, the fundamental frequencies. One would expect the military communications to be higher, which they were. At the end of it, the most is -- we could say is that it remains possible, an open possibility, that the three speakers in the military intercepted communication were Obrenovic, Krstic, and Jevdjevic. For completeness, I should perhaps say that I normally work with a scale of opinion which has five positive points and five negative points. On the positive -- in the middle of the scale, there is a neutral point which is point zero where I rested in this particular case. I'm saying it's possible, point zero, that it's the questioned speakers. Above that there are five positive points where I say point plus 1, it's rather more likely than not to be the same person; point plus 2, fairly likely; 3, likely; 4, very likely; and in a very, very small minority of cases where one has copious high-quality recordings and perhaps speech impediments or something like that, there's point plus 5 which I perhaps evoke in 0.05 per cent of cases - one case in 200 - where I'll say I'm sure. So effectively, it's a four-point scale; the fifth point is seldom evoked. On the negative side, the scale is a mirror image of itself, so point minus 1, rather more likely than not that they're different speakers, down to minus 5 where I'm saying I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, [redacted]. Thank you for that analysis on the voice comparison. On the technical side of the comparison, the spectrogram and the other technical aspects, you did that yourself, all by yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's correct. For limited parts of it, looking at, for example, fundamental frequency, Witness EE was present, and I would describe to that witness what was there on the computer screen and we would discuss it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into your report and your analysis of the -- between the two tapes and whether or not there was any indications evidence of tampering or authentication analysis, as we've called it. And we're both obviously speaking the same language. We need to slow down a bit so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I do apologise. Perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, just before coming to, I can point out that there is an error in the report that we've just referred to, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: This is in the speaker identification report, 840/A, the one that's just been produced -- no, sorry, that's the curriculum vitae. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you would be looking to --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Page 2 of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- 839/A, "Examination of Speech Samples."

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It could be. I don't have one with a number on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You should have one with a number right in front.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, one is on its way.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, this is 839/A. I turn to page 2 of that report, page 2 being the first text page after the cover, looking about a quarter of the way down the page to the second major heading, which says: "2. Material Examined and instructions," five lines down under (i), I say: "An Agfa brand open spool audio tape..."; and on the next line, under (ii), I say that: "A BASF brand open spool audio tape..." In fact they should be reversed; it's tape 32 which is the BASF brand and tape 48 which is the Agfa brand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: The second exercise that I was asked to undertake involved examining the two versions of the recording for any evidence of them having been edited or tampered with. I just wonder if it's possible to have an indication from the interpreters as to whether this is the appropriate speed for delivery?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We hear from them that it's not, so I think you're doing just fine.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: All right, thank you. To assist me with these examinations, I was provided firstly with the two tapes themselves; secondly with a transcript in B/C/S of the conversation and also with a translation of it into English. In addition to that, a Mr. Jack Hunter, who works for the visual information branch of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms in the United States, sent me various things, including a preliminary report that he had made concerning his inspections of radio interception equipment, and also Uher tape recordings which I understand had been used to record from the intercept equipment; a further report which concerned his, if you like, slightly more detailed investigations of those items, some photographs of those items, and also three spools, open spools of audio recording tape which he'd used to make some experimental recordings on from Uher tape recorders which I understand had been used in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- how much of Jack Hunter material did you rely on in your tamper analysis?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Very little, very little. I was given certain information to help with the examinations. Firstly, I was told that the first recording to come to light had been the one on tape 48. Once the recording on tape 48 had come to light, the transcript had been made of it, and it was only at a later date, I think in some archives in Sarajevo, that it was explained to me that tape 32 had been found during the execution of a search warrant, and it also transpired that tape 32 contained the same recording as tape 48. It was explained to me, and this was consistent with the information contained in Jack Hunter's reports, that at the time of the war, different intercept stations would be intercepting sometimes the same conversations, and it appeared from examining the tape, the two tapes, that this is what had happened here, and I'll explain why in a moment. When I examined the tapes, I found that the questioned recording on tape 48, that was the first one to come to light, was to be found at around 20 minutes and 15 seconds into the running time of the tape. The version which was on the second tape, tape 32, appeared at around 12 minutes and 50 seconds into the running time of the tape. On both tapes, the questioned recording appeared partway through a series of other recordings of a similar kind; so in other words, both tapes appeared to contain, if you like, a succession of military radio intercept recordings, and in both cases, the questioned recording appeared partway through that succession. When I looked at the recordings in a bit of detail, it appeared that they had been recorded firstly at a running speed of 4.7 centimetres a second, that's 1 7/8 inches a second, which is speed that Uher tape-recorders do record at, and both of them were in monophonic rather than stereophonic, half-track format. In other words, the magnetic track on the tape extended from near to the edge to about the halfway point. The physical dimensions of the tracks were similar to those on the test recordings supplied by Mr. Hunter. The tapes both showed evidence of quite a lot of wear. The appearance was that they'd been used and reused and used and reused, and tape 32 in particular, when it was examined under a microscope, showed quite a lot of scratching to the surface of the tape. When I compared the tapes with -- the recordings with one another, I found firstly that there was a slight difference in running speed, that if I synchronised the two recordings and recorded them within a two-channel system of a computer, tape 32, say, in channel 1 displayed at the top of the screen, and tape 48 in channel 2 displayed at the bottom of the screen, and I synchronised the starting points of the recordings and the waveforms, by the end of the recording, it was clear that tape 32 was slightly ahead. After the 2 minutes 29 seconds running time of the recording, it appeared that tape 32 was ahead by just under 2 seconds, 1.94 seconds, which suggested that tape 32 had been recorded on a machine with a slightly slower running speed than tape 48. So if it's recorded in playback slightly slowly [sic], it will appear slightly speeded up in playback. This is quite common, that you'll find two instances of the same make and model of the machine which are supposed to run at, say, a nominal running speed of 4.7 centimetres a second, but in reality, particularly when they've had quite a lot of wear and tear and use, they -- one will start to run more quickly or more slowly than the other. Another difference between the two recordings was the strength of the voice signals. If we remember, these are two-channel radio communications. In Mr. Hunter's report it's suggested that what happened was speech would be broadcast on one transmission frequency, and the acknowledgement or the reply would come back on another frequency. And the scanners, the receivers that were being used to intercept them, would be tuned to one frequency only, and one would achieve a good, clear quality or louder signal from the channel or the frequency that one was tuned into. The replies coming from the other channel would either be non-existent or they would be less loud, the signal strength would be less, and this is consistent with experiments I've done on radio frequencies for a previous case. In the two recordings in question, the one on tape 48, the speech attributed to Obrenovic was stronger, was of greater amplitude than that attributed to Jevdjevic and Krstic, their being at the other part, the other side of the communication; and in tape 32, the position was reversed. In other words, Krstic was louder and so was Jevdjevic, and Obrenovic was the more quiet of the two voices. There were differences in the opening sections of the two recordings. In the tape 48 version -- it would help me if I might use the, I think you call it an ELMO to project from the transcript and to explain what I mean on this point. May I do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think you'll get some help from the usher, and that's Exhibit 789/A, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Exhibit 789/A which is tape 48, which is, again, the first -- the tape that first came to light.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. This is the transcript of the tape 48 version of the recording, and here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to need a little adjustment for the ELMO so we can get in the relevant parts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just give me a moment to look at another version of the transcript before I, before I move on with that? Would it be possible to do this from the B/C/S version of tape 48 as opposed to this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly. And that should be underneath it as 789/B, or close by somewhere.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's the one. Yes, in this version here, the tape 48 version, it wasn't entirely clear to me whether the recording began at that point there just before "Obrenovic sa Palme," or whether it began two lines later, around ten seconds later, because we have here at the beginning of the recording what could be the switching transient, the click sound for the recorder going on; but here at this line there are three further possible transients, three further possible clicks, which could indicate that that is not the beginning of the recording but this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. French, for the record, when you point, if you could just explain where you're pointing so the record will accept it as opposed to "this" or "that."

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'll go through that again. At this point here we're about 20 minutes and 15 -- sorry, at line 1 of the transcript we're at about 20 minutes and 15 seconds into the running time of the tape. Just prior to line 1 there's a click sound which could be a switching transient. A switching transient is a click resulting from a surge in electrical energy introduced onto the tape by the turning on, in this case, of a tape-recorder or by the release of a pause button. At line 3 of the transcript, some ten seconds later, there are three further click sounds which again could be switching transients. They could be on clicks of some sort or another. Without access to the specific recorder which had been used to make this recording, I really couldn't say whether the beginning is here at -- that's just prior to line 1 at 20 minutes and 15 seconds, or some ten seconds later here at line 3 of the transcript. With regard to tape 32, the position is a little more complex. What appears to be the case with tape 32 is that the tape-recorder has been left running in the record mode. In other words, the record button has been pressed, but the pause button has also been pressed, too, if you like, possibly in readiness for the making of a recording, so that if one were to hear a recording that one wished to go onto the tape, a conversation that one wished to go onto the tape, all one would need to do would be to lift the pause button. So it appears that the recorder has been left in the record mode but with the pause button depressed, and about midway on the page, just prior to the word "momenat," the pause button has been lifted, thereby recording the word "momenat" as the first word in the tape 32 version of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just, for the record, establish that tape 32 is Exhibit 835. And perhaps on that third arrow that you've written down there, which is where you're telling us tape 32 started, could you just put a little 32 there so that will give us a reference that this is -- instead of bringing out the other transcript right now, this will just help us.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Okay. I have done that. What appears to happen, then, is that the pause button is lifted, which allows the word "momenat" to be recorded. But after the recording of the word "momenat," the pause button is again depressed, it's pushed down, stopping the tape. It's only stopped very briefly, I think for 1.35 seconds, which is the time in which the word "halo" occurs, which is attributed to Krstic here, just below "momenat" on the transcript. But by pressing the record button, what happens -- sorry, by pressing the pause button, what happens is when that person is saying "halo," the recorder is stopped; therefore, the "halo" doesn't go onto the tape. The pause button is lifted immediately after "halo" and the recording continues as on the tape 48 version. So just to be clear on that, on the tape 32 version the "halo" doesn't occur, and I'm going to strike it out just for the record. The tape has the word "momenat" on, and then the next thing that one hears is the person claimed to be Obrenovic saying this line here, which I can't pronounce because I'm not a B/C/S speaker, "sta" -- whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you, just for clarity, if we see Exhibit 835/B, which is the tape 32 section that is missing this particular part. They should have it. They will bring it up.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I have a version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's use the one with the exhibit on it, is our practice.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I think it is the one with the exhibit on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you've got it, great. Let's use that one. If you could just go to the B/C/S section and point out what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: If I could put the two side by side, it might clarify it. Yes, please. That one and this one. Are they both on the screen there? Let me align them. No. It would be easier if I just -- there we have it. You can see them side by side. This is the tape 48 version. We see "momenat," "halo," and then this line here, the line below "halo." On the tape 32 version there is no "halo" because the pause button has been pressed after "momenat," I think, and then lifted, and then the recording continues. But by the action of pressing the pause button, one bypasses the recording of this word "halo." It's omitted. The recordings then continue in parallel and the contents are the same until we come to the end sections. On the tape 48 version, after the conclusion of the conversation, there are a series of beeps and what sounds like radio equipment disconnection sounds. On the tape 32 version, those don't appear. The recording finishes before those occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do you conclude that the "halo" is missing on the one version because of the pause button? How are you able to make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: On two bases: There is a click there which has a particular shape when one looks at the wave form. On some recordings sent to me by Mr. Jack Hunter, he had made experimental recordings in which he had been lifting and putting down the pause control on a newer tape-recorder. There were clicks on those recordings associated with the action of using the pause button which was similar in shape to or in configuration to the one that occurs at that point on the tape 32 version. The second reason is I made an experimental recording on another Uher 4000 tape recorder, the type I was given to understand had been used in Bosnia, and I too found a similar shape of click; not identical, but similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you also have a chance to briefly question one of the intercept operators about their practice?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. If we could be careful of the --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I do apologise. I hope that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Keep going.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: The intercept operator that I spoke to gave me the information that it was common practice when monitoring conversations to have the Uher tape recorders running in the record mode but with the pause control down so that the tape wasn't actually recording. It was at points when they heard something worthwhile that they would left the pause button and record onto the tape. Now, very often, he tells me, once radio contact between two people had been established, the person initiating the contact or initiating the transmission, would say, "Could I speak to Major X?" and the voice at the other end would say, "momenat," or "moment, please." What they would then do, they would press the pause button again, because sometimes it might take 10 or 15 minutes, he told me, go and get the person concerned, and then when that person came on the line, or they could hear them coming on the line, they would lift the pause button. So in the light of what he told me, the pausing of the tape recorder after "momenat" would be exactly where one would expect it to be paused, perhaps in anticipation of a long wait before the person he's asked for comes to the transmission equipment. But in this case, there wasn't a long wait; the person was almost immediately there, hence one explanation for why the "halo" is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any other sort of reasonable, more suspicious explanation for these clicks and the various things you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I couldn't really, on a common-sense basis, conceive of why somebody would want to edit the word "halo" out of the tape. It would seem to me to be one of the -- to be a benign feature of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could just continue your analysis.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. In the position of Mozart; too many notes. With the exception of the click and the missing "halo" in tape 32 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're through with the ELMO for a while.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, would this be a convenient moment to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure it is, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a 20-minute break. We adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. French, if you could just continue where you left off in your tamper analysis.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I left off almost, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. French. The microphones got turned off.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I was just arriving at my conclusions, I think, before the short adjournment, which were, firstly, that with the exception of the -- what I believe as a pause transient after the word "momenat" in tape 32, the recording signals in both tapes appeared to be continuous. In short, I can find no evidence of either of them having been tampered with or edited. Now, having said that, I should just add a caveat, which is that nowadays it's usual for an audio expert to say, and this is quite correct, that the failure to find evidence of editing doesn't necessarily imply that the tape definitely has not been edited. And the reason I say this is because there are nowadays available digital systems, computers, whereby one could record a conversation from a tape, re-record it from a tape to the computer, and then, within the specialised sound analysis or sound processing or editing programme of the computer, one could edit up the recording, deleting sections perhaps, whatever, and do this more or less without trace. The edits are almost seamless if they're done in a very competent way. And the material could then be re-recorded back from the computer to a tape and passed off as an unedited version of the recording. In other words, it would be possible, I believe, and I think most other experts working within the field would nowadays say so, that it would be possible to produce an edited recording which has defied forensic detection. However, there's a very unusual aspect to the present case, in my experience, and that is that two versions of the same recording have become available at different points in time. One is not a copy of the other and they can't both be copies of the same original recording. In view of that, I have to say that the possibility of digital editing having occurred, I must say I see it as much, much lower, significantly lower than, one would have to say, in a normal case. For it to have occurred, both of these recordings - I can't see any alternative to this - would have had to have been edited independently of one another and in exactly the same ways. And I think the work and skill that would go into that would be extremely great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If one was to create a conversation like this, if you were asked to create a conversation like this, how could you do it?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: With the assistance of actors, perhaps, or people who were simply going to adopt the roles of those they were projecting into. I must say, in the past I've had a number of tapes which have involved actors who've got -- not actors, but people who have got together in order to improvise conversations, perhaps reading from scripts, perhaps just improvising as they went along, in order to manufacture evidence for a tape-recorder which is later being presented in court. In those cases, it has always seemed to me perfectly obvious that the performance, the language has been wooden, it has been stilted. In the present conversations, there are at least three areas of overlapping speech, and because of that, this appears to me - and I'll come on to the issue of being a non-speaker of B/C/S in a moment - but this appears to me to have the sort of messiness that one would associate with natural conversation, that is, two people talking at once or overlapping in their speech. In addition to that, having worked with Witness EE on this, who is a speaker of this language and who has research knowledge of the dialects, I did consult him on this issue and asked whether the conversation appeared wooden or whether it appeared stilted or play acted, and the answer came back no. I also did ask a native speaker and a linguist of this particular language as well, a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Besides just excellent actors overlapping speech, what else would have to be created to give the same kind of tonal qualities that we hear on these tapes?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Well, it would have to be done over radio transmission channels and recorded over them, or at least over some kind of electrical and electronic circuitry that mimic their characteristics. It would be a very elaborate hoax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that if a person had a library of several conversations of particular people that they could take individual words and phrases and splice them all together on this computer and make completely fake sentences? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I have seen in a previous case a tape which was -- exactly that had been done with it. When one read the transcript of the conversation, the conversation appeared entirely normal; it appeared to flow. When one listened to the tape, however, it was a joke. I mean, there were two aspects to it: One is having the right words in the right order, but the other aspect is making it sound like phonetically and phonologically that the words are on the right pitch, the intonation is correct, that the cadences -- and so on and so forth, and that is very difficult indeed. It can be manipulated within a computer system. One can manipulate the pitch, the intonation, et cetera, but it is still a difficult task, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what is your final opinion about these two particular tapes regarding whether they've been tampered or faked?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I can find no evidence of tampering or faking, and I think those comments must be bore -- interpreted in the light of what I've just said about the difficulties of play acting and montage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Visnjic, I see it's Mr. Visnjic who is going to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. French.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, in your report, exhibit number 838, on page 2 you say that the tapes that you examined were received in your laboratory on the 9th of November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time you saw those tapes?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I believe so, but if I can just consult my records. I've certainly had copies of the tapes -- copies of the conversations before that. Is your question these physical tapes, these actual ones rather than copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My first question would relate to the actual physical existence of the tapes that you now have before you.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: "Momenat." Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you receive copies of those tapes earlier on?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber when you received those copies?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd of February in 1999. And that was a copy only of the recording from tape 48, plus some other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you prepare any preliminary reports on the basis of the copies, those copies, those that you received in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to work on some preliminary findings on the basis of those copies?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It was possible to do some preliminary work. At that point in time, I was working not with Witness EE but with another linguist who was, in fact, a native speaker of B/C/S. But as time went on, it became clear that I needed a different collaborator.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the same page, page 2, you say, in the last paragraph, that joint investigation between you and [redacted] was carried out at your laboratory in York in the week from the 19th to the 26th of November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is the week when myself and Witness EE examined the recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Witness EE -- do you know that he saw the tapes for the first time then?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall. He may have had a copy of the recordings prior to our meeting in York. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, did you know whether these tapes had been given to any other expert; and if so, did anyone else work on an expert finding, a forensic examination, and are you familiar with the results of those examinations?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: As far as I know, no such examinations took place, unless I wasn't told about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On November 1st, 2000, at a hearing, my learned friend Mr. McCloskey stated on pages 6803, 6804 of the transcript, that this copy of the audiotapes had been given to an expert and that the Prosecution has for months been trying to get hold of a final response from the expert. Bearing this in mind, do you assume that that perhaps relates to you or to somebody else? Because this was on the 1st of November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I really feel it isn't a matter for me to say what was in Mr. McCloskey's mind, but it could well have related to me. I know of no other expert that's been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. French, on page 6 of the English version of your report on the audiotapes, Prosecution Exhibit 838, paragraph 4, "Editing and Tampering," you explained that modern devices make it possible to do some editing or tampering. My question is the following: Could digital technology, which you assume might have been used, did such technology exist in 1998 and prior to that period?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Certainly it existed in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On condition that all the technical requirements existed, those that you referred to regarding editing and tampering, on the basis of your own experience, would a period of six weeks be sufficient to do such montage or editing?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Well, the problem with it is that you would have to do it on two versions of the same recording in exactly the same way, and if one were to be chopping out sections and inserting material from other recordings, one would have to do it in exactly the same way in two versions of an original recording, getting the timings exactly, precisely the same in both -- or not the same, but relatively the same. If you remember, one tapes runs slightly faster than the other. Am I saying too much?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, perhaps we didn't quite understand one another. I quite understand the procedure that you just explained to the Trial Chamber. My question is: Could that whole procedure have been completed in a period of six weeks?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I think the question maybe should be whether it could be completed at all, rather than within six weeks, to produce this. I really don't -- can't comment on the time scale that would be needed. All I can say is that, in my view, to produce these two recordings would be an extremely difficult feat, in six weeks or any other time scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could six weeks be used as some kind of framework for doing this, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It would depend upon the sophistication of the technology, the skills of the manpower, how many people were involved, whether or not one had sound engineers, perhaps phoneticians, computer operators. I really can't answer the question in the abstract without knowing about the circumstances of that sort, really. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. French, in your report -- or rather, you received a Mr. Hunter's report?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the report dated the 23rd of March, 1998. I don't know if you have it at hand.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I think I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, before I put my question to you, may I just say or ask whether Mr. Hunter is also familiar with the actual technology of tape collecting, examination, and so on? Is he an expert in the area? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what his background or expertise or experience is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In his report of the 23rd of March, 1998, page marked 00889128, this would be the page 2 of his report, actually, in paragraph 4, the last sentence says that all recordings were of good quality.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Could you just give me a moment to reread this report in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I'm not clear which recordings he's referring to in the end of paragraph 4. You see, the recordings that he refers to there clearly are not these tapes because these tapes were recorded at a running speed of 4.7 centimetres per second, and none of the recordings that he refers to there were recorded at 4.7, so he is clearly talking about other recordings. If he is, I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But it is a report which refers to the reception of the first 19 audio open spool tapes, one of which is in front of you, the tape that you received first marked as 48.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I really can't be accountable for Mr. Hunter's work, but the recordings on that tape are not at the speeds he lists here. They're at 4.7 centimetres per second, and they're not of good quality. Whether Mr. Hunter has overlooked that or not listened to all the recordings or perhaps -- I don't know want to impugn him in any way. I really don't know what he's seen. If you're telling me that this was among the first -- sorry, among the first 19, or what you tell me or what I read here doesn't square with what I found on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And if I may repeat what you say in your report on page 3.3, that the tapes were of poor quality. This is the report?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, they were of poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. French, in your report on the audiotapes, on page 3 of the English version, under (vii), you say that Mr. Hunter gave you three audiotapes, open spool Ampex brand audiotapes containing experimental recordings which Mr. Hunter had made on Uher tape recorders?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, also in Mr. Hunter's report, dated the 24th of April -- we have a large number of documents, but we'll go through them slowly.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, I have his report in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to paragraph 7 from the top, page 2.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Could you read the first words of that paragraph to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "At the site I requested to see --"

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I have it, yes, yes. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hunter says that he took experimental tapes for all the machines that he had, and then he identified those tape recorders with numbers from K1 through K7.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: He did the same on the next page, page 3 --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- where at the other position from which allegedly conversations were intercepted, he also took specimen tapes and marked another three Uher tape recorders.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question, Dr. French, is, on the basis of the samples provided to you by Mr. Hunter --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- were you able to determine the tape recorder on which any one of these tapes was taped?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: No. In fact, that would have been a very large enterprise to try and -- to try and do that. I think I still wouldn't be here with my final report. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But each of these machines has a specific result on the tape; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Not necessarily so. There are a couple of factors here. One is that it is by no means -- research has by no means established that each individual tape recorder has its own unique signature or fingerprint. That's the first aspect. The second aspect is that I did have a conversation with Mr. Hunter, and he did tell me over the telephone that it was possible that none of these recorders had recorded the tape or either of the tapes, that in fact machines might have been scrapped. The other thing that he told me is that the recorders that he looked at, that some of them - and I think he based this on his interviews with personnel in Bosnia - had had repairs to them and perhaps even to the heads of the machines. So even if one of those machines had been used and even if it did have some individual characteristics, there would have been no guarantee that at the point at which he saw it or found it, it had the same characteristic that it had when these tapes were made. It really would have been such an open-ended exercise to try and tie either one of these tapes down to any of the recorders that it just was not embarked upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, from the scientific point of view, is it easier to identify the machine, the tape recorder, or the speaker? Which is more precise?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Neither is precise, and I couldn't given a weighting of the precision to one relative to the precision of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, let us go back to the report on the audiotapes, Exhibit 839.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. 839 is the examination of speech samples; 838 is the report on audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself. It was speech samples that Defence referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was a misinterpretation, but I was referring to the report on speech samples, OTP Exhibit 839.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, on page 4 of the English version of your report --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- the last paragraph -- it is page 5 of the Serbian version, paragraph 2. Allow me to read this sentence: "Owing to the non-equivalence of the known and questioned samples (normal voice vs raised voice), the most one can say from the voice quality comparisons is that they failed to eliminate any of the three known speakers." Dr. French, could the same conclusion be the same as saying that not one of the known speakers was confirmed?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes. It's a question of the Prosecution perhaps saying that my glass is half full and you would say it's half empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, we're still dealing with the same report, but let me ask you: Do you know, are you aware of the International Association for Identification? Are you familiar with that institution and the standards adopted by that institution for speech comparisons?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I'm aware of some of those standards in outline. I'm aware of the existence of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of the English version of your report, under 3, under the heading "Observations and Results," you refer to the technical quality of both versions of the tape.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also, and quite rightly so, stated that there was very little speech energy found at frequencies above 1.7 kilohertz.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that some institutions -- or rather, that the standards of the International Association for Identification is such that tapes that have a lower frequency, below 2 kilohertz, are considered absolutely unsuitable for making any kind of comparisons because they are technically of poor quality?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I would say two things in relation to it. One is, firstly, that the organisation that you refer to is by no means an internationally accepted one, particularly within the European forensic speech community. Indeed, its activities have caused a few eyebrows to be raised. Secondly, I would point out that in order to -- what one is not concerned with is necessarily identification. As an objective, impartial scientist, my task in this case was not to identify your client or his colleagues; it was to determine whether they were on the tape. In other words, when I do these examinations, I have in my mind the possibility of elimination just as much as the possibility of identification. And the importance of that remark is this: that it is sometimes possible to eliminate speakers if they have very different voices from the ones on the recording with very poor quality material indeed. One needs rather good material sometimes for identification, but for elimination one can often work with recordings of this type. For instance, if someone has a very different voice quality or dialect features or whatever, or one person has a speech impediment or a pathology of their voice or something of that sort, even on very poor quality recordings, that can show through. And if that is not on the other samples that one is comparing it with, it is very important, even with poor quality material, to go through with the possibility of elimination. So I would not accept, I would not accept that standard, and nor would, I think, my colleagues in the European context, or most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. French, that, for instance, the FBI laboratories do not do these comparisons with tapes whose quality is below 2.5 kilohertz?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that, but if that is the case, I can't see how they can be proceeding with the view of elimination in mind, as well as identification, as equal possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your expert report, on page 5 of the English text, under the heading of "Pitch/Fundamental Frequency Measurements," you list some of the elements which lead to a change in the height of the tone of the main frequency, or pitch of the main frequency, and one of those elements would be a raised voice. Am I correct in making that assumption?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Anger, fear, or sorrow, in one and the same person or speaker, can they produce characteristic differences in fundamental frequency?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: They are just a few of the things that can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is that also true of stress, emphasis, semantics, intonation of words and sentences, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Are you asking whether those emotions can affect intonation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Emotions do affect intonation. I don't think it affects semantics. Semantics is the study of word meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The way in which words and sentences are enunciated, the speed of speech, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Would be subject to emotional factors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: With one and the same person, would there be a difference in fundamental frequency of speech, from morning till night? That is to say, if we look at it over the course of one day, would fundamental frequency be the same throughout for a given speaker?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It might or it might not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If the same text were repeated again and again by the same person, could there be a difference in fundamental frequency?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: There could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May we then conclude that part of your report measuring pitch/fundamental frequency measurements, shows in actual fact that there is no similarity between the basic sample and the comparative sample, and that there are numerous reasons for that or that numerous reasons can exist?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, one could conclude that. The reason for doing the fundamental frequency test in this particular case is, as you quite rightly say, when a person has raised their voice, they raise their fundamental frequency. The two go hand in hand. This was established in the earlier part of this century first by a French phonetician known as Etienne Lombard, and Lombard noted the phenomenon whereby if a person raised their voice, perhaps against a background of noise, they raised their pitch as well. So with raised voices, one finds raised pitch or raised fundamental frequency. Now, the importance in this case was simply as an elimination test, as stated.
