We have General Krstic talking in a reasonably calm and deliberate way in his interview recording. We have a man shouting in a radio recording. One would expect the radio recording, if it were the same person, to be higher, but also a variety of other people would do it higher as well. But crucially, if the person -- if the known sample, the interview recording of your client was higher than the person with obviously raised voice in the radio recording, the intercept recording, then that would be at least a basis or a partial basis for eliminating him; hence, the necessity to carry out the test with the view not only of identification, but elimination in mind, too, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On condition that the known sample was performed under conditions in which that person was not under stress or anger, emotional changes or similar things. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: No. You can tell from the known sample that the person -- I don't know what internal stress they were suffering. I mean people, some people have enormous internal stress and emotion, and they don't reflect it much Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in their voice. Others might be under a small amount of stress and emotion, and they do. All I can say is that I look at the interview recording and the person is obviously not raising -- it's a not "dobro! dobro!" You know, it's not like that, whereas the person in the military recording clearly is talking in that way. If the necessity to do the test is the person who has clearly raised their voice, going back to Lombard's research, if they turned out to have a lower fundamental frequency than the interview sample, then that would be very important. It would be very important for your client. Whatever the effects, the emotional effects of the interview, your client had not raised his voice in that way; hence the necessity to do the fundamental frequency check.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But the conclusion of the test, the fundamental frequency test is nonetheless inconclusive; am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, on the last page of your report or the addition to the report, you give a scale of judgements --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- and it follows a certain logic of determining degree.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Under -- or rather, can you tell me what the difference is, or rather, is there a scientifically defined difference between, say, 2 and 3 on your scale? Is it a percentage of similarity or on the basis of similar words, or what are the elements that go towards determining this scale?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: The first thing that I should say is it is not an interval scale. It is not a numerical linear scale with equal points between each of the numbers; rather, it is a scale which is shared by the majority of forensic phoneticians working in the UK context. It is similar to the one in use in the state laboratory here in Rijswijk and in the Bundes Criminalsamt Laboratory in Germany, and so on and so forth. But at the end of it, it is really a measure of personal confidence in one's judgement, and that's what it is. It is subjective in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Following on from the logics of this scale of judgements, if we look at the zero position, it states, if I'm right, that it is possible that X and Y are the same speaker. Now, bearing in mind one of my previous questions, would you agree with me that a possible definition is, "I think it is possible that X and Y are not the same speaker," by the same token?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: With the corollary of that statement at point zero, it is, in my view, possible that X and Y are the same speaker would be as a corollary that they are different speakers. That would be possible too. I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dr. French, may we then conclude that your eight-page report in fact leads to a conclusion which in English could be termed inconclusive?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: An inconclusive conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, your witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. French, did a Defence expert have a chance to come to your laboratory and review this material, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I don't have the specific date in front of me, but a Defence expert did come to my laboratory and examine the material in the presence of the gentleman who has just been cross-examining me. I could get the particular date. My recollection is it was about two to three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Mr. Visnjic came along with the expert to your laboratory?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's right. And the expert, a Mr. Koenig, or Koenig as Anglicised here, from the United States, an ex-FBI examiner who is now a private expert, came along with Mr. Visnjic and carried out examinations of the recordings and made copies of them and took them away as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long were they with you?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: From 10.00 in the morning until 5.30, with possibly a gap for lunch, an hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're aware that Mr. Koenig has testified in this Tribunal as an expert for the Defence in a case?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. French, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I've been listening with great interest to your very knowledgeable expos‚, and I would just like to have some clarification which you can perhaps give to a layman.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As I see, you mentioned that there is an open possibility that the three speakers were the same.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when discussion with the Defence lawyer, you said that of course you can always say that a glass is half empty or half full, of course if it is exactly half, half, 50-50. Now, then, you can say that also there is an open possibility that the three speakers are not the same?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: One could say -- I couldn't say it was an equal possibility. I could say that it's possible that it is the three people it concerned, but there is an indeterminate number of other people, other males within that population. I couldn't put my -- I couldn't specify how many that it could also be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, there are possibilities of identification, and there are possibilities of elimination?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is more accessible to you? Is it easier to eliminate, or is it easier to identify?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: One can eliminate on the basis of less material and poor-quality material if it obviously is not the person. For example, if there was a very poor quality recording of my voice and Your Honour's voice, both speaking in English but very poor quality and very brief, I don't think a forensic examiner would have any difficulty in distinguishing between us. If, however, our voices sounded very like, we spoke English with the same accent and the same sorts of resonances, a forensic examiner on the basis of a poor-quality recording or a brief recording would be rather circumspect about producing an identification. So it is easier to do an elimination on the basis of poor material or scant material if the people have different voice characteristics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you spoke about the fundamental frequency test which -- does this -- could this test lead sometimes still to identification?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Not in itself, Your Honour, no. It would -- it's only one test which is used as an indicator with -- among a much larger battery or package of tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in our case it was inconclusive?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It was inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in many cases it is conclusive?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: It can be conclusive in elimination. For example, I've just concluded a case for the moment for the Prosecution in England where there is -- there are recordings of a youth speaking over a telephone line, reporting an arson. He set fire or somebody -- they believe the caller has set fire to a building and then phoned the emergency services for a fire engine to come. He's clearly speaking on raised voice. One can hear noise outside the telephone kiosk and his voice is raised. The suspect in interview is speaking in non-raised voice, yet the fundamental frequency in the interview was higher, and on the basis partially of that, I would eliminate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So your tools for elimination are more at hand?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: In this case one could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now speaking of the possibility of a montage, you mentioned that one tape would run slightly faster than the other. Would this be any -- indicative of any tampering?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Oh, no, Your Honour. One could take several different instances of the same make and model of tape recorder which had been subject to different degrees of use and wear. None of them would run at exactly the same speed spot on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you mentioned that certain features were benign features, like the difference in clicks and the differences in the opening sections, but then you mentioned something about the strength of the voice signals. And in that regard, you -- comparing, comparing the two tapes 48 and 32, you said that the speech of General Krstic was louder than Obrenovic, and in tape 48, the speech of Obrenovic was of greater amplitude.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: The same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Now, does this entail that there could be two different people?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Oh, no, no. It's clearly the same recording, Your Honour. No, no, I think not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was nothing in the timbre of the voice, difference in timbre or --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Nothing that I noticed at all. It was simply we have two recordings. On one, one end of the radio channel is louder, but on the other recording, the second end of the radio channel is louder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But what you call the voice quality is the same?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: As far as one can assess, it's the same recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the rhythm of speech?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think I have no other questions for you, but definitely there is a lot to learn from what you said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: You're very flattering, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Dr. French, is there any way to tell whether two tapes, like tape 48 and 49, were made in roughly the same time period, or is that just totally outside the --

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: No. I couldn't tell you that, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: There's no way that I would know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. You said that -- you gave the zero on the rating scale, evaluation for recognition of the voices of all three of the participants: General Krstic, Jevdjevic and Obrenovic. Do you know, or could you tell us, or was there any -- within that scale that you gave them all zero, were any of those voices -- was the degree of confidence in any of those voices higher than in the other two or the other one?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't. It was about equivalent for all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you a hypothetical, with which I'm sure you're very familiar, having testified in court. You told us all the difficulties there would be in trying to recreate a tape like this after the fact and how your experience had led you to believe that -- or in some other instances it was kind of easy once you listened to the tape -- not kind of easy, but it was not impossible to discern that it was indeed a play-acting. But let me just hypothesise and see if you would have this -- if it would be as easy in the following instance. Suppose this was -- I say, again, totally suppose. Suppose it was not a recreation, but suppose somebody wanted to set somebody else up originally, and they initiated a regular intercept, and then, by prearrangement, they had somebody else take the place of one of the people - we'll use as an example General Krstic - just had another person step in there and take. And I suppose the motive might be something like disinformation. At some point in the intercept, they say, "The Turks are probably listening to us. Let them listen." Would that be as easy to discern as the later created or would it all depend on how well the actor was playing that one role?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if one had a reasonably good actor who sounded rather like General Krstic, I think it would be possible, yes, for that person to play-act this conversation with the other person, possibly one person believing that -- one person acting out a real conversation or thinking it was real and the other one just fitting in. You would need someone with a similar sounding voice and also somebody who knew, I suppose, the sorts of things that people said in these military radio conversations, and I suppose one would have to get them into a position where they could broadcast and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Dr. French, I would like to go back to the question raised by my distinguished colleague Madam Judge Wald a moment ago. If you were asked to recreate a conversation like the one we have, how could you do it - and this is what Mr. McCloskey was asking - but in giving us -- that is to say, could this be done in a completely confidential manner? That's the first point. How many people would have to intervene to accomplish that task, and could all that be done in the same laboratory or would you have to involve other participants from different places, if I can put it that way? Well, those are my questions for you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: I think the answer to that is -- would be dependent on how one was going to construct it. One possibility that Mr. McCloskey put to me was that there was a sort of library of tape recordings of General Krstic, of utterances, and that the -- how likely would it be that someone could pick a sentence out here and a word out there, and yet another sentence from a third tape and five words from a fourth tape and six words from a sixth -- and so on and so forth, and put them together to arrive at this conversation. Now, to do that would really be a mammoth task. I mean, once we start getting into that area, I think one is moving nearer to American, with due respect, Your Honour, detective fiction than the forensic reality of it. But to, say, have a recording of this sort, where one was simply deleting the odd word and then rejoining it within the computer and re-recording the tape would be much -- considerably easier and it would involve less in the way of resources, manpower, personnel, et cetera, et cetera. But the thing is, one would have to recreate the two tapes which have the same sequence of words, they have the same time base except one runs slightly faster than the other, so on and so forth. I really don't know how many people one would have to involve or -- I imagine the second scenario that we're talking about now could be done within one laboratory. Yes, well, I could do it. A gamekeeper turned poacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time would you need to do that?

utterances.speaker: PETER FRENCH
utterances.text: Just to delete the odd word and then re-record it to a tape? It would depend how much I deleted, but to do that I could perhaps do it within a day. Except in this case one would have to do other things, such as, well, intersperse it within a whole series of other military conversations on two different tapes. No, it would take several days, perhaps. I don't know. I really -- it's open-ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Thank you, Dr. French. We thank you very much for coming here to the Tribunal. You have clarified many points to the parties and to the Chamber as well. We should like to thank you profoundly for coming and wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence, and every success in your work, which is fascinating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a good time to take a break. Our next witness will require some protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before taking a break, if we may, Mr. Petrusic, could I ask you, with respect to General Krstic's health, would you like to have shorter breaks, that is to say, shorter working sessions and shorter breaks - for example, 45 minutes of work with a 15-minute break - or do you prefer us to go on working for one hour, 20, and then have a 20-minute break, or one and a half hours with a 30-minute break? How would you like us to work, in view of General Krstic's health? If you don't wish to answer now, you could talk to the General, perhaps, ask him during the break, and then come back to us with your answer after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. After the break, we shall inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. For the time being, let us take a 50-minute lunch break at this point. Let us adjourn for 50 minutes for lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to make a solemn declaration now. I'm not quite sure how you're going to do it. Do you have a braille edition of the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've memorised the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. So please make the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Make yourself as comfortable as you can. Thank you for coming, and first you will be answering questions which Mr. McCloskey is going to put to you. But before we start with that, I beg your pardon for a moment, it is necessary for you to confirm your name on a piece of paper, but I don't know how I'm to do that. Perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, you could help us. As you are a protected witness, and you will be known as Witness EE so we can't use your name, but you need to confirm whether we have your name correctly. Perhaps if anybody is going to utter the name, we should switch off the microphones. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I see that you wanted to say something. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, I'm ready to go when you are, Mr. President. I just wanted to confirm, are we in closed session? Okay. We're not in closed session yet, so it's my understanding that the usher whispered the witness's name in his ear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but allow us to hear from Witness EE whether the name that the usher whispered to him was indeed his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The usher did not whisper my name in my ear; he told me what my alias is. I'd be happy to write down my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, that will be fine. I think that is a good way of proceeding. We'll begin with the testimony by Witness EE. Mr. Petrusic, have you any response to my previous question prior to lunch so that we can organise our time and make the breaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Having consulted General Krstic, the Defence would suggest that we preserve the same rhythm that we applied up to now, that is, a break before lunch, a lunch break, and then perhaps we could divide the rest of the time after lunch into two as well and have another break in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Mr. McCloskey, we will have a ten-minute break more or less halfway towards 3.00, if that suits you. Either you tell me, or I will give you a sign. So please begin, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could go in closed session for the first part of the testimony. We've talked to the Defence about this, and it will be evident why. Yes. Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now, so you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And before we get into the -- some of the relevant dialects, let me just ask you, do you -- based on your studies, have you travelled extensively in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you just give us, oh, just a brief description of how often you may have visited there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I visited the former Yugoslavia at least -- for research at least six or seven times. The most extensive stay was when I -- in 1989, 1990, when I spent 13 months researching for my dissertation and travelled -- worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the institute for language and literature in Sarajevo, Institut za Jecik e Knjizevnost, and also at the Bosnia-Herzegovina academia of arts and sciences, and I also spent a lot of time researching at the Serbian academy of arts and sciences in Belgrade. Since then, I had two more research trips after the war in 1997 and in 1998. 1997 took me to Belgrade, and 1998 took me to Bosnia again, to Sarajevo and its environs, to Belgrade and to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Based on your studies and your knowledge, is it possible to identify indicia of ethnicity from listening to the speech of a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes. My feeling is that you really have to be very knowledgeable about the language in order to be able to do so. I think a layperson or a person -- or average person might not notice all these differences, but when you study and learn a lot of the dialect studies, and there were many written about ethnic dialects, dialective Muslims or dialective Serbs in this particular area, let's say, of Bosnia or of Croatia, then you begin to note some of those small but still, I would say, audible differences between -- I mean, among the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. And having that in mind, can you explain to the Court what the Prosecution asked you to do, and what you were able to do; and if you can provide us with just your rough conclusions, and then you can go through and support those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: The Prosecution asked me to examine tapes which -- with -- and I had both the tapes and the transcripts of conversations that were attributed to some officers in the army. They were attributed to General Krstic [redacted] [redacted]. And I was asked to analyse under laboratory conditions these speech samples to see if I could identify any of those characteristics which might distinguish these speakers as either of Muslim or Serb or Croat, perhaps, origin, and I tried do this as objectively and as honestly as I could.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And who did you work with in that project?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I worked with Dr. French.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you've reviewed the overall report that you and he co-authored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you've seen his final evaluation for the speech part of that report, reflecting his zero result?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes, and I would concur with it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could tell us, were you able to identify any particular ethnic speech tendencies from any of the three speakers on the two tapes that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes. I have to make one caveat, that the speech sample is rather short; but even in such a short speech sample, I was able to find a few tendencies which make me make some -- draw some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what were your basic conclusions, and then I think you will be able to explain the tendencies you saw in the speech.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Well, my basic conclusions are that the speakers reveal some features typical of some ethnic Serb, either dialects or ethnic -- or Serb speech from Serbia itself. I did not find any what I would call classic Muslim speech features which are spoken about in many of the dialect studies.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you please now just tell the Court what your examination of the two tapes revealed, what tendencies did you see, and just explain it as you would your class?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps I'll use this overhead, the ELMO for that, if that's okay at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And let us make sure it's up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, I think we can -- this is OTP Exhibit 847, and the two or the three yellow dots are there to assist the witness and don't have any significance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: May I -- is this now visible to everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Well, the basic division in this former Serbo-Croatian speech territory is the three main dialects. I'm only showing you one of the main dialects; that's why there's an asterisk. I'm showing you the Stokavian dialect which is the largest of the dialects of this area. The other two dialects, Cakavian and Kajkavian, are purely Croatian dialects and do not interest us in this particular instant. The main or traditional subdivision of Stokavian is into these three subdialects, Ikavian, and now I'll point to ijekavian, which is here, ijekavian, and ekavian. These differences are based on the pronunciation of a vowel that was inherited from an earlier version of Slavic. I will not be focussing on Ikavian in this presentation because Ikavian is limited to Western Bosnia, Western Herzegovina, and Central Dalmatia, and there's no signs of Ikavian at all in the speech sample that I have examined. What is also interesting to see from this exhibit is that the ekavian form is spoken exclusively, I would say, or almost exclusively by Serbs, especially in Serbia in the Federal Republic of Yugoslav. The ijekavian form of the dialect is spoken by many -- all four ethnic groups of the former Yugoslavia that spoke Serbo-Croatian, so we have Muslims, Slavs, Croats, Serbs, and Montenegrins. However, there are some differences, more complicated, and there's some more stratification among these ijekavian speakers which I can go into later if need be, but there are some differences, say, between the speech of Serb, ethnic Serbs from Bosnia in their ijekavian speech and, say, ethnic Croats or ethnic Muslim Slavs from Bosnia, and I can go into those in a bit. What is most striking perhaps for me in the speech samples that I reviewed is that there is a mixture of these two dialect types in the speech of, I believe -- certainly of what is attributed to Obrenovic, Major Obrenovic, and what is attributed to General Krstic. They often use -- in some words they use the ekavian form, which would be consistent with what would be used in Serbia or even among Eastern Bosnian Serbs; and in other instances you find ijekavian forms. Now, let me, just to help the Court explain where we -- how significant differences of these three dialects are. I'll give one word, or two or three words, perhaps, from each dialect group and show you the differences. I'll try to enunciate them as clearly as possible. So the word for milk, for example, in Ikavian would be "mliko," in ijekavian would be "mlijeko," and in ekavian would be "mleko." The word for girl is slightly different: Ikavian, "divojka"; ijekavian, "djevojka"; ekavian, "dejvojka". One last one because it does actually occur in our tape, in some positions there's a slight other difference. Ikavian, which would be the word, the past tense of to live, "zivija"; ijekavian is identical, would be "ziveo" with an e-o; and ekavian would be "zivio." So that's I think -- I hope I haven't bored the Court too much with my analysis of these three dialects.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So can you tell us now as you went through the tapes, were you able to pick up any speech tendencies, patterns, pronunciations, and identify them as possibly Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Well, one of the first things I did is I noted in some of the conversations, and not in and among all the speakers simply because I didn't have enough time -- enough speech material from all the speakers, but I noticed some features which placed -- at least, seemed to place these speakers in Bosnia. One of the features in Obrenovic, what is attributed to Obrenovic's speech, which is about 53 seconds on the tape, we have three times the use of a tense called the aorist tense, which is not standard -- not frequent in standard use. The examples would be "izgubi," "rece" - "izgubi" meaning lost, "rece" being sad - and "rekose," which would be plural, they said. This would be, if you know French, this would be sort of equivalent to having active use of the passe simple. So this is typical especially of the speech in Bosnia, so this for me was an indicator that there was some linkage to Bosnia. As far as characteristics, there is a mixture here of both ijekavian and ekavian in the speech samples, which are consistent with one of the dialect studies I consulted specifically for the Serbs of Eastern Bosnia. So, for example, in the word "here," which in Serbo -- in this language is "ovde" or "ovdje," the speakers consistly use the ekavian form, "ovde." Same with the word for "where"; "gde," or "gdje." Consistently we see the use of the ekavian, "gde." On the other hand, we do have some ijekavian forms, which would be indicative of a potential origin in -- to the west of the Drina River, and there we have such -- one form is "cijevi" is in the tape. That's an ijekavian form. Ekavian would be "cevi." And "vjero vatno" in ekavian would be "vero vatno." So these are some -- there are more features, which we could go into later.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness EE, would you expect ekavian speech patterns in a Muslim in this situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Normally not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is it possible, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: It might be possible if a Muslim from Bosnia spent time, say, in Belgrade or in Serbia, and it is possible that they might have picked up some ekavian features. But my feeling is that once they would return to Bosnia, they would go back to their ijekavian way of speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What specifically can you tell us about the speech on the tapes attributed to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes. General Krstic has -- in the speech attributed to General Krstic we have only about 28 seconds, but there are a few things that I picked up which I think are significant. In the line in which he says -- the speaker says, "Don't leave a single one alive," the first time I believe it's, "ni jednog nemojte ostaviti zivoga." We see a form of prohibition, and as I have told you earlier, this was something I have researched quite extensively, which would be typical of speakers west of the Drina River, meaning in Serbia - I'm sorry. Strike that - in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia. It is the use of the infinitive, "ostaviti," after a prohibition particle, "nemoj" or "nemojte." Now, when that line is repeated, however, more emphatically, it seems to me, where it's, "ni jednog zivog nemoj da ostavljate," the form has changed, as you can tell, if you have the transcript, and no longer are we looking at a typical west of the Drina form, but what I have found in my research to be typical of Serbs in Serbia, and Montenegrins, which is the loss of the infinitive, "da ostavljate," and also the reduction of the prohibition particle from "nemojte," which is a plural, which was in the line above, to a singular, "nemoj," and this is something that I have documented and have found this same phenomenon in a variety of dialects from, I would say, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would this be something you would expect to see in a Muslim speaker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I had a questionnaire on specifically this form which I had passed around to Muslim speakers of Bosnia, and they indicated that they would not use that particular form.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you'd like to highlight as significant speech tendencies of General Krstic or any other speakers in the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think that one another feature that needs to be spoken about is the status of a phoneme "h", which has been indicated in many of the dialect studies as being more frequent, more frequent -- now, that doesn't mean it's absolutely there all the time, but more frequent among Muslim Slav speakers, and that the Serb speakers have tended more often to lose that phoneme. And I have found in the speech sample that the phoneme "h" is lost in several places. All three, I believe, all three speakers on the tape have lost it, and especially in the word, say, "ajde," instead of "hajde," which is "come on," which was also, by the way, a subject of my research. I looked extensively at the dialects for that one. And also in the -- there's one, I think, what we call genitive plural, "gori nema," "gori nema." I think it should have been "gorih nema," with an "h." So there is evidence also in the word "hello," "alo" instead of "halo," that the "h" is lost or the "h" sound is lost. This suggests again that the speakers perhaps were indeed of Serb ethnicity rather than Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you mentioned that you relied on studies, dialect studies for that area. Can you just briefly tell us the time period those studies were conducted and the ethnic origin of the authors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Okay. That's quite an interesting subject. From around 1970 through the beginning of the war in 1992 in socialist Yugoslavia, there were at least 18 or 19 studies that I'm aware of that are of ethnic dialect rather than of geographic dialect, so that the writers of these dialect studies looked specifically at the speech of particular ethnic groups, be it Serb, Muslim, or Croat. So within Bosnia I believe - I can check this on one of my articles - I believe I counted at least 14 such what I call ethnocentric dialect studies. So I've used many of those. I've looked at all 18 of those studies, actually. And I've looked also at specific dialect studies for specific regions. One article I have is about Western Bosnia, another article is about an ethnically-mixed area in Croatia, and recently I've also looked at two dialect studies specifically for Eastern Bosnia, one of which is the dialect of Serbs of a town in Eastern Bosnia, the town of Kladanj. And another one is the dialect of Muslims of the town of Tuholj, which is right near Kladanj. And so I've been able to compare those two studies and see what are some of the differences posited specifically for eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who authored this study of Kladanj Serbs that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Professor Slobodan Remetic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And is he a respected Serbian expert in this field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the other studies that you talked about, the pre-war studies, did you find them at all jaundiced by nationalism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think the subtext of some of these was nationalism. However, I think that the experts who prepared them were serious linguists who did, I think -- of course, they vary in quality, but I think some of them are really of high value and I think that there was a tradition, especially, say, in Serbia, of high standards in dialectological research.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've had a chance to review a report of a Defence expert in this case, a Mr. Simic. Having reviewed that report, do you find it -- have you chosen to respond to anything in particular in that report that you think needs to be brought out in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: To a great extent I believe we have some similarities in our conclusions. One thing I might want to clarify, which might not have been clear in my own report, is about the East Herzegovina dialect. What I probably should have written in that report is that the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even of Croatia, speak an East Herzegovina-type dialect, which means it's not identical with what is currently spoken in East Herzegovina, but it had probably gone through some local modification but is based on East Herzegovina. For evidence of that, I have looked at a book published 1984 in Sarajevo called "Phonological Descriptions," "Fonoloski Opisi," and specifically, two villages or two locations in Eastern Bosnia, the town of Zepa and Milici, the village, I guess, or the town of Milici, are said to have East Herzegovina characteristics. So that's one thing I want to clarify based on that report. So I'm not necessarily saying that the speakers on the tape speak the way that they would speak in eastern Herzegovina, but they display some eastern Herzegovina characteristics. The other thing I would like to respond to is the notion that there are only minimal or non-existent differences among the speakers, especially in the context of the Yugoslav People's Army or JNA. I think that certainly we're mixed nationalities in the JNA, but that most of the -- many of the officer corps were of Serb ethnicity. Now, not the majority, but certainly -- maybe not the majority. I'm not an expert on the military, but my understanding is that a good number of the officer corps were of Serb origin. It seems unlikely to me that if -- well, certainly -- let me rephrase that. It seems that if these speakers were members of the JNA and they have a mixed ijekavian/ekavian speech pattern, the way that the Defence report speaks of it, then this actually helps my thesis that the speakers on the tape were probably of Bosnian origin or perhaps ijekavian dialect origin who have spent time in Serbia or in high positions in Serbia where ekavian dialect was more frequently used in the army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you find any indications of classic Muslim speech tendencies or patterns in the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: No. One thing that is apparently characteristic of ethnic Muslim speech is not only the preservation of the phoneme "h," but occasionally also the addition in words where it wasn't supposed to be of the phoneme "h." So that, for example -- again, given the short speech sample, there were no such words, but on the other hand there was also no tendency to preserve "h" among the speakers. In addition, the merger of the affricates or consonants which the language admits, which are "che" [phoen] and "tch" [phoen], a kind of hard and soft "che" [phoen], these were not -- there is quite extensive literature which tells us that Muslim Slavs in Bosnia tend, but of course not all of them do it, tend to merge these two phonemes, and there was no evidence of the merging of these phonemes. These phonemes were well preserved in the text, in the speech samples that I reviewed. I think there was one other feature I wanted to talk about, and I -- it has now slipped my mind. I might get back to it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That's okay. Besides the two military-type tapes, or those fuzzier tapes that you were listening to, you were also provided with clear tapes of the various parties. Did you use those tapes in your analysis in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I certainly listened to them, but the quality is so different, and also I think the context was so different. Speakers in a more formal context are likely to use a more standard form of the language. And in the context of the tape, where this is not a formal context, they tend to bring in more dialect forms. Occasionally in some of the -- well, quite frequently, actually, in the speech samples from the testimonies here, I did hear that "h" lost, but perhaps in some instances it was preserved, and that is a difference, I think, in style. When you're trying to speak a more literary form of the language, you will, from your schooling and education, you will insert those elements. I think we all can do that kind of code switching in any language.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I don't know if you wanted to speak to the issues of the differences of the "cha" pronunciations. If that was not the one you were thinking about just ignore that question, and if you think you've got it all, then if you could briefly summarise what you were able to gather from these two tapes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Right. My overall conclusion is that, given the limited time, limited period of speech, limited -- I mean, the fact that these speech samples were so short, I could notice some tendencies which made me believe that the features here were more often associated with speakers that are of ethnic Serb background rather than any other ethnic background of Bosnia or of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness EE.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this would be a good opportunity to have a ten-minute break, so we're going to have a ten-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, you are not going to restart?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've spoken to Mr. Visnjic, and the witness has recalled the last point he wanted to mention, and it should be very brief. If he could just recall to the Court his last point, and Mr. Visnjic and I agreed that that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, if you could tell us about this last point that you just recalled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes, it is relatively minor, but it's still something I confirmed in the two dialect studies from Eastern Bosnia, that the Serbs of Eastern Bosnia lose a J sound or a "yot" sound between two vowels, and this is something I heard quite clearly on the tape. I heard the form, it is good, or "dobro," without the "je," without the "yot"; while in the neighbouring Muslim dialect, apparently that "yot" is preserved. So there is another minor, but still if you listen for it, you can hear that little difference. That would be the thing that I had forgotten to mention earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recall who was speaking on the tape that you heard this tendency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think it was definitely the voice attributed to Obrenovic, and I would have to review the tape one more time to make sure, but I have a feeling it might have been also the voice attributed to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness EE. You are the only expert witness who understands our language, and therefore let me ask you to make pauses between question and answer to give the interpreters a chance to interpret us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness EE, have you appeared as an expert witness before, before the Tribunal with respect to an analysis of voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Not before the Tribunal, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness EE, if there are two individuals who were brought up in the same environment, grew up in the same environment, they lived in a similar social surrounding, would they speak differently on the basis of their religion or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think you would need to clarify what you mean by the same environment. Are you talking about two people who are potentially neighbours in the same area, or people maybe in the same town but who live in different neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I am thinking of the same area. Hypothetically, let's look at Eastern Bosnia. Let's start off with that, Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Well, one of the interesting things that I found, they could be from the same region but speak differently, and this is confirmed in dialect studies of Eastern Bosnia that I have read, one by Senahid Halilovic about the dialect of Tuholj, there could be -- and the other one that I mentioned earlier about the Serb dialect of Kladanj. So there can be differences. They're from the same region, and they speak somewhat differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I assume that they can come from different -- originate from different areas but speak the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you mean by "different areas"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Referring back to the study you mentioned a moment ago about the Serbian dialect in Kladanj, is it possible for Serbs from Eastern Bosnia, one from Kladanj, for example, and the other one from Zvornik, or two individuals not necessarily Serbs, that they speak with the same linguistic characteristics, speak in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Right. I understand your question. Well, I have looked at a more general dialect overview, it's called Pregled Srpskohrvatski Dijalekata, and actually in that specific dialect study, written by a professor from Belgrade University, Asim Peco, there is mention of more general characteristics of all of Eastern Bosnia, not just these two points, say Kladanj and Tuholj, in which he does distinguish between the speech of Muslims in that area and the speech of the Orthodox population in the area; so, yes. One particular thing that is noteworthy for Eastern Bosnia is that the Muslim population can display in some parts, at least, what is known in our profession as an archaic Eastern Bosnia accentuation, which means they have some accents that are not, not the same as in, say, standard -- the standard language or in the East Herzegovina language which became one of the standards of the former Serbo-Croatian language, and Asim Peco addresses this in his study.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about social status, education, other social elements? Do they lessen the gap, this distinction, or increase it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: That's a very good question. I think that in most, most cases, education could have that effect indeed, but what I would like to argue and what is true even of my own, let's say, American background is if I speak a native dialect, let's say of Chicago, and I try to learn -- speak -- through my education, I pick up a standard American dialect, not a Chicago, then when I'm back in Chicago I will tend to speak like a Chicagoan. Similarly, I believe that even with education and even with high education, if somebody has picked up the standard dialect, when they are back home or in a more comfortable surrounding or a familiar surrounding, they will code switch and use their more native dialect, and it also could happen when they get more emotional or when they get into more rapid speech or when they're talking to their parents, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness EE, is it possible that a Bosnian Croat, a Bosnian Serb, a Bosnian Muslim speaks the same? Can they all speak the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: It's a theoretical question. It depends where and depends in what context. I think that it's entirely possible, say, in -- before the war, that in Sarajevo, urban centre, you might not have been able to tell the differences among the three groups; however, if you go into the provinces, you tend to be able to hear more of the differences. And one of my studies was particularly of Western Bosnia where I looked at Croat speech, Muslim speech, and Serb speech, and I identified sort of what I called seven primary speech features which are used which have been said to differentiate these groups. With the new reality of these three separate languages, Croatian, Serbian, and Bosnian, today, for example, a Bosnian Croat is likely to use more forms from standard -- from the new Croatian. So that could be in terms of words or lexicon, say, they might say instead of "avion" they might say "zrakoplov," which would mark them; or they will say "poduzece" instead of "preduzece," et cetera, et cetera. "Avion" being airplane, "poduzece" meaning -- I can't think of the word, sorry. I'm blanking on the word in English, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Thank you, company. "Kazaliste" and "pozoriste", for example; theatre. There's some of those. As far as the Muslims, one of the features which might distinguish them even in an urban setting might be their more frequent use of "h." There's been a big push in Bosnia to have the Muslim speakers today, for example, use "h" much more frequently even where it's not supposed to be, such as in a form like widow, "udovica," where the Bosnian Muslims actually say "hudovica," and that "h" has no reason for being. It's never -- it never was there and should never have been there, but it is there. Similarly with the word for coffee, "kafa," Muslims might say "kahva," right now as in the new political realities of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This last portion, I have understood as something happening now, how new languages or a new language is being developed. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes, but if we're looking at speech samples from after the breakup of Yugoslavia, we have to, to some extent, take that into consideration. Prior to the breakup of Yugoslavia, there were already some -- quite a few differences between the speech of Croats and Serbs, and also the Muslims would vacillate. They would use, say, in Bosnia they would use some Croatian pronunciations, but they'd use some verbal forms or some what we call lexical items or simply vocabulary words which were of Serbs origin, so they had a kind of mixed speech. And -- but you could still see, according to the dialect studies, and I've looked at many written in the 1970s and 1980s, and even in some urban areas like Tuzla and Visoko in Bosnia, where they are differentiating Muslim speech from other speech patterns. And that's before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the situation in Eastern Bosnia where the vast majority of the population - and we've heard statements from different witnesses about this - was economically and educationally focussed on Serbia. And many people who were heard here as witnesses actually worked in Belgrade. They were either construction workers or work in different companies. So do you allow for the possibility that the use of their -- or the fact that they had spent a significant portion of their time in Serbia and the fact that the border is nearby, close by, and the fact that by their education and training and their military service as well, that in their speech, in the way they speak, the differences that you are talking about have been considerably lessened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Frankly, I believe that that would, to a great extent, depend on individuals, and again, I think it's a question of code switching. If these people lived extensively in Serbia or worked in Serbia but would come home frequently to their parents and their family and their relatives in Bosnia, that they would preserve or even return to the native -- their native dialect. You have to realise that I think to great extent -- I mean, I've known a lot of people in Belgrade who have lived there for many, many years, don't have too many relatives outside of Belgrade by now -- and I'm thinking of Montenegrins, for example, who have totally adopted ekavian, and certainly if it's a second generation individual whose parents might be ijekavian speakers and they live within Belgrade, that the children will adopt what's in school and speak ekavian. So it really -- I think it depends on the individuals, but I wouldn't be -- I wouldn't venture to guess on a general tendency. But my feeling is, given what I know about socio-linguistics in many regions of the world, including the former Yugoslavia, that people are good at code switching, that you never do forget your -- necessarily your native dialect, and that even if you have influences from other dialects, you might, when you are back in your native environment, you would revert back to your native dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And a native dialect for the Serbs in Eastern Bosnia, it is ijekavian, am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Yes, the native dialect for Serbs is ijekavian; however, however, there was a lot of pressure in Republika Srpska for Serbs to adopt ekavian of Belgrade. And this admittance of ekavian of Belgrade is a kind of -- one of those links that might link them, these Serbs, to their kin across the Drina River in Serbia, and for that reason, there might be some conscious reasons to want to maintain ekavian because ekavian is identifiable with Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that people are conscious of the difference in pronunciation, that is to say, whether they're speaking ijekavian or ekavian, and can they correct the difference or speak differently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think there was an increased awareness about this over the years. I'll give you a few examples from my own experiences when I would travel in different parts of Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, and might slip into -- my own dialect that I studied was ekavian, and when I would travel to Croatia, I would be corrected. People were aware that I was speaking ekavian and identified it as Serbian. When I was in Serbia, since Serbs speak both ijekavian and ekavian, I didn't get into that trouble if I happened to slip and use an ijekavian form, but that rarely happens. That's from personal experience. Remind me, please, of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that people are conscious of the difference in pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: It would be difficult to make a generalisation, but I think that many people could very well be, but this is based on my feeling rather than necessarily on something that I have spent a lot of time studying, and also from personal experience. I've talked to a lot of people who have moved around and have gone, say, to Belgrade, especially when I was there in 1998 and spoke to some Serbs from Bosnia who were in Belgrade; they maintained their ijekavian pronunciation quite clearly and quite deliberately. They said they really don't want to switch. They feel that that -- but their children are already totally ekavian speakers. So I think -- and also many people in Belgrade at the time said that since there are so many refugees from the other parts of the former Yugoslavia, that ijekavian is used quite a lot and that they notice these differences. So I think the differences are noticed. Whether it's noticed if an individual makes a political -- quote unquote, political statement by speaking ekavian or ijekavian, there is some precedence for that. We know the examples of especially Bosnian Serb political leaders trying to force themselves to speak ekavian, not always very successfully, but that was something that happened for quite a number of -- for a few years, especially during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if the individual wishes to give the impression that he or she is a Bosnian Serb, in their speech they will, of course, use partially or wholly the ekavian [Realtime transcript read in error "ijekavian"] dialect? You can say yes or no, give us a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was it ijekavian or ekavian?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ekavian, "E."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase the question, because that made a difference for me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that an individual who wishes to give the impression that they are talking like a Serb, will that individual in their own speech consciously use elements of the ekavian, e-k, ekavian, either partially or wholly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Okay. I read -- there was a major controversy in Serb linguistics about the status of ijekavian after the decision by the Bosnian Serb leader at that time to declare ekavian as a language, as the dialect, official dialect of the Serb-held areas of Bosnia; and this individual, I think his name was -- well, I don't want to make a mistake, so I won't tell you right now but I've got it in my notes. This individual said that most Bosnian Serbs would speak ijekavian, but that intellectuals or those who want to make a point and show that they are true Serbs, and they were not a large number, would only speak ekavian, and not a mixture of ijekavian and ekavian. Now, I should point out one more thing, that the dialects of Eastern Bosnia, as I said in my earlier testimony, are basically ijekavian, but they have many ekavisms, many ekavian features that are native to that region. So there are two possibilities here; that these speakers of Eastern Bosnia had a few ekavisms in their native languages, or that they picked them up through travel or through their time maybe in the Yugoslav People's Army or working in Belgrade, say, or any other part of ekavian-speaking Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that refer to speakers who can be Muslims and Croats as well but originated from Eastern Bosnia? Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: The literature shows that the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, the literature that I have read, have fewer ekavisms in their speech and often they don't have -- they're certainly much less frequent in their speech. And specifically, in the words that I have found in the tape recordings, I found a variety of other forms that had -- did not have the ekavian reflex. So such as in the word "ovde" or "gde," I found -- in some villages or some areas I found "dje," which is indicative of ekavism, and I found "ovdje" or "ovdi" even, but not "ovde."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The frequency of the use of ekavian can be the result of military or police training; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness EE, how much time is needed, in your opinion, and you said something about this at the beginning of your testimony when you were explaining the phase of the disintegration of Serbo-Croatian into separate languages, how much time, in your opinion, is necessary for this separate language to be formed? I don't know if I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I would like a clarification, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned as a general question for consideration the disintegration of the Serbo-Croatian language into separate languages, and my question is, how long does that process last until a final version of the language is formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long does this take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: It's impossible to predict, but what I can tell you is that the process did not just begin in 1991. The process had begun already, I would say -- well, there are two things I could say. We already have an example of a separate Croatian language which was part of the fascist state of Croatia, '41 to '45, which of course Croatian was declared the official language, and a pre-1892 orthographic system was imposed on that territory. But more to our point, already in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and throughout, the Croats had been forming a separate language and had actually declared in the declaration on the position and name of the Croatian literary language that Croatian is indeed a separate language. So that process has been going on for -- well, had been going on for at least 20, 25 years before the breakup of Yugoslavia, and is likely to continue. And I'm not a prophet, so I really can't say for how much longer. With regard to the Bosnian language as a separate language, I would say that that process began with the 1974 Federal Yugoslav Constitution, which allowed for greater language rights among the different republics that spoke Serbo-Croatian, and one of the things that happened as a result was that the republic, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted a standard linguistic idiom for the republic which was slightly different, say, than the western, meaning Zagreb, or the eastern, meaning Belgrade, variant of the language. So we sort of have an embryo of today's separate Bosnian language, and as nationalist forces gained power in the '80s, those moves towards a separate Bosnian language were accelerated. Now, of the three languages thus far emerged - Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian - Croatian is ahead of them all in forming its own separate language, and I think we still have to see where the Bosnian and Serbian different languages will go. But as I said, normally these things take at least a generation because you've got to train a whole cadre of school children in the "new language."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness EE, during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned that if somebody spent a longer space of time outside his environment, it is possible that he can take on the characteristics of speech of that region; but when they go back to their original region, the characteristics and this influence from outside is lost. Now, my question to you is the following: How much time is needed for an individual to go back to his original way of speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I would like to just make one correction to what you just said. I didn't say that the older characteristics are immediately lost. I meant to say that the person is familiar with both ways of speaking, but it seems to be almost an instinctual thing for that speaker, upon return to the native environment, to revert to what I've called the native dialect of that speaker, and the influence of that other speech pattern that they might have picked up lessens. It's not an absolute yes, the minute you come home you lose it, but it certainly, over a short period of time, I would say - and I can't venture to guess how long. I mean, it varies from individual to individual - that they are likely to code switch and use their native dialect. I think we all, to some extent, are capable of doing that, and there's quite an extensive linguistic literature about code switching and bidialectalism and how this works. Some people have referred to it as home language versus work language, or home language versus outside-of-the-home language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I assume that the period is, say, less than three years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Do you mean the period of returning to your native dialect?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Precisely that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Much less than three years, I would have to say. And of course, I have to add the caveat that there could be -- it does vary from individual to individual. I would think that this is something that in many individuals is probably just a given characteristic of code switching. It's well known that speakers of a dialect are able to code switch, either between their native dialect and the standard language, or their native dialect and another dialect they might have picked up when they were living elsewhere. I would say it's definitely -- well, most definitely in much less than three years I would think there would be a return to a more native form of speech. Again, also I might add, it depends. If that person spends only a week at home and then returns, it's another story. So these are all hypothetical questions which I think to some extent might depend on the individual. I really can't venture to guess how long it would take for any given individual. It would be wrong of me to try and venture a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the transcript of the conversation which is the subject of your expert report, the word "bolan" is mentioned. This word is characteristic for those belonging to all three ethnicities in Bosnia. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure about the Croats, but I certainly can vouch for the Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness EE. Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, any additional questions? If you have, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your review of the evidence tapes, of the fuzzier tapes, did you notice any bad acting, any awkward, wooden moments, anything that might lead you to believe this was a put-on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness EE.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You highlighted the idiosyncracies between the way of speech, especially between Muslims and people of Serb ethnicity, indicating many words, the "h," and the "j," "yot," and so on. Suppose somebody wanted -- a Muslim wanted to imitate the speech of a person of Serb ethnicity. Would he find any difficulty to overcome these obstacles? As much as a French would like to imitate a German, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I think it would be quite difficult. I think they would have to have adequate -- an expert to train them on doing that. I don't think it's something that they would naturally be able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it can be detected. If one of -- one ethnicity, especially Muslim, tried to imitate a Serb ethnicity, an expert can detect the nuances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: I believe so. What I found in these texts is that -- in these transcripts - I'm sorry - in the tapes was a kind of consistency which made me believe that these people were authentic rather than acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in your overall conclusion, which you said that the features were more often associated with speakers of ethnic Serb background, you think it is a very firm conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EE
utterances.text: Well, I would have felt more comfortable had I had a longer speech sample, but given what I had, there were, I think, enough clues to help me come to that conclusion. As an academician, of course we need long speech samples, but given the limitations of what I had, this is the conclusion that I have reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. I see that Madam Judge Wald has no questions, and neither have I. Therefore, we wish to thank you very much, Witness EE, for coming, and we wish you a safe journey and success in your future work. Please don't move for the moment, because we have to bring down the blinds to protect your identity. We will meet again tomorrow at 9.20. For now, the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
